headline: Southwest Ledge Still Holding Cold, Clean Water — Bass and a Strengthening Fluke Run
subhead: The current stalls at the top of the ebb and you can feel the whole Ledge breathe — bass are still down there, and the fluke bite is building fast.
body_markdown:
There's a stretch of water right at the top of the ebb on the Southwest Ledge where everything just stops moving for a minute — the boat sits dead still, the rod tips quit dancing, and you can practically feel the whole Ledge exhale before the tide turns and starts pulling the other way. That's the moment I wait for every trip out there this time of year. The water's still clean and cold enough to hold fish tight to the structure, and that stand of the tide is when the bigger bass show themselves before the current picks back up and pushes everything into the rips.

That's the story of Block Island right now — the water here is doing what it's always done for us in July, staying cooler and better oxygenated than the mainland beaches, and the bass know it. While stripers from the Jersey shore up through the western Sound have gone nocturnal, hunkering down in the low-to-mid 70s water and only really feeding after dark, our fish don't need to run that program. The current ripping over the Ledge and through the North Rip keeps things stirred and cool enough that we're still getting a legitimate daytime bite, especially on the stronger stages of the tide. I had a 38-pounder come off the bottom in about 55 feet on the west side of the Ledge on a bucktail-and-eel combo last Thursday morning, broad daylight, nothing subtle about the take. Southwest Ledge and the rips off Southeast Light continue to be the go-to structure — tube and worm trolled slow through 40 to 60 feet on the last two hours of the ebb has been the most consistent producer, with live eels taking over once the sun starts dropping and the bigger class of fish moves up onto the shallower boulder fields to feed.

Bluefish are mixed in wherever the bass are working, and some of them are legitimately heavy — I've seen a few in the 12 to 14 pound range busting bait right on the surface off the North Rip on calm mornings. If you want a change of pace from bass fishing, throwing poppers or Hopkins jigs into a blitz like that will wear your arm out fast, and it's about as much fun as this fishery offers.

The fluke run has been building steadily and it's worth making the trip for on its own right now. Drifting the sand-and-gravel edges off the west side of the island, along the approaches to the Great Salt Pond and down toward Charlestown, has been putting keeper fish in the box consistently on the incoming tide. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom with just enough lift to feel the structure, has been the ticket — and we're seeing enough size mixed in with the shorts that it's turning into a real target species rather than an afterthought while you wait for the bass bite to turn on. This is shaping up to be one of the better fluke seasons we've had out here in a few years, and the pattern's still building, not fading.

Porgies are doing what porgies do — thick on the reefs off the southwest corner, biting sea worms and clam on light tackle in 20 to 35 feet whenever the tide's moving. It's not glamorous fishing but it's about as sure a thing as this island offers right now, and it's a good way to fill a cooler on a day when the bigger stuff isn't cooperating.

Further offshore, the canyon boats running out of here have been finding a legitimate recreational bluefin window — fish in that 27 to 47 inch slot working over sand eels and small bait, with yellowfin starting to mix in for crews pushing to the deeper canyon edges. That's a longer run and a different game than the inshore stuff, but it's worth knowing it's out there if you've got the boat and the fuel for it.

No bonito yet, and I want to be straight about that rather than tease something that isn't here. The water's been climbing into the range where they'll eventually show, and squid are building in the protected coves around the island the way they do right before the false albacore and bonito scouts arrive — but the honest read is early-to-mid August before we see the first fish crash bait on the surface here. I'll be watching the coves off the southwest corner and keeping bait rigs rigged just in case, but I wouldn't plan a trip around them yet.

Looking ahead, the tide is easing toward the July 21st first quarter, which means softer current stages through the rest of this week. That usually means slower presentations produce better — less speed on the troll, more patience letting the eel or tube sink into the strike zone before working it. If the current stays manageable and the wind holds out of the south or southwest without kicking up a mess, I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb on the Ledge for bass, then shift over to the fluke grounds on the building incoming. That's the play I'm making this week, and it's given up good fish two out of the last three trips — solid odds for late July, but you still need to be on the right stage of the tide when it happens.
